newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - VW gets larger share of global market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - VW gets larger share of global market.

text.p: Volkswagen AG, profiting from a gamble on international sales, said on Tuesday its global deliveries rose to nearly four million vehicles in 1996, making the German carmaker the fourth largest in the world.

VW said worldwide vehicle deliveries rose to 3.966 million units in 1996 compared with 3.560 million in 1995, giving it 10 percent of the global passenger vehicle market in 1996 compared with 9.4 percent a year earlier.
The gains were impressive in the weak European market, where VW reported vehicle deliveries excluding Germany of 1.39 million vehicles, a gain of 14.7 percent for the year.

Prospects for higher 1997 sales, as well as an increase in market share, will be pinned on the launch of the new Golf as well as other new products, including a mini-car dubbed the VW Lupino and intensive marketing efforts, VW officials said.

But the higher foreign sales, which included a 41 percent gain in eastern Europe, were dampened by a meagre 2.6 percent increase in domestic sales to 969,400 vehicles at a time when Germany's total vehicle sales rose about five percent.
The lacklustre performance in Germany lost VW some of its domestic market share, which slipped to 19 percent from 19.4 percent in 1995.

But it was still ahead of Adam Opel AG, a unit of General Motors Corp, at 16 percent, with whom it ended in early January a bitter four-year-old feud over charges of industrial spying when it lured away production guru Jose Ignacio Lopez.

Industry analysts said the weak German sales were in part due to the planned rollout of a new Golf model in late 1997, prompting some buyers to put off making a new purchase of the workhorse car that has long been a steady performer for VW.
Other factors were hefty sales incentives offered by Asian manufacturers, mainly from Korea, that many German carmakers did not match, which helped to erode market share.
"I am not unhappy with the sales developments since they stepped up market share in Europe at a time when the Golf is due to be replaced," said HSBC James Capel analyst Bob Barber.

VW management board member Robert Buechelhofer told Reuters in an interview that the German market in 1996 was "extremely competitive" with hefty incentives by some carmakers. Another reason was the priority on international sales.

"We hope we can reverse the trend in 1997. We will of course also try to provide the right supply for the German markets since part of our supply in 1996 was directed into international markets," Buechelhofer said.
But VW's strategic offensive into international markets, aimed at reducing the carmaker's reliance on Germany, was successful as most regions posted double-digit growth.
Buechelhofer said vehicles from VW's Czech subsidiary Skoda were "the right product" for eastern Europe, where deliveries rose 41 percent to 225,500 vehicles.
Sales in the vast North American market, where VW's vehicle deliveries surged 19.4 percent to 241,900 units, were helped by product repositioning and revamped communication strategies.
"We implemented a breakthrough strategy in North America and it worked out nicely," Buechelhofer said, noting the carmaker would seek to keep up the pace of expansion in 1997.

In Japan, Buechelhofer said VW found success with its subcompact Polo, which was introduced into the market in mid-1996 and received aggressive marketing help. VW's deliveries in the country rose 32 percent to 59,100 units.
